title: The scholarly-weight census — how much serious scholarship exists, and of what kind
framingVersion: docs/FRAMING.md v2 (the quotation amendment), as amended 2026-07-30

hardLine.statement: This file measures ATTENTION PAID BY SCHOLARS to a body of text. It measures nothing else. It does not rank, score, or imply how well any rite works as magic; it contains no efficacy field, no effects field, and no place for either. A corpus with a century of philology behind it is a corpus that has been READ carefully. It is not thereby more true, more powerful, or more likely to do anything. The Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā has the strongest critical edition on this list and no demonstrated operative validity whatsoever; so does the Papyri Graecae Magicae; so does everything else here.
hardLine.governingInvariant: FRAMING §1.1 — frequency of attestation is evidence about transmission, never about efficacy. This census extends that: DENSITY OF SCHOLARSHIP is evidence about a modern academic field's priorities, never about a historical claim's truth.
hardLine.documentedEffects: none recorded here — out of scope for this axis. No physiological, psychological or toxicological finding appears in this file. Effects belong to the harm-note apparatus (FRAMING §5.1) and to the sibling toxicology slice, not to a bibliometric census. Do not join this table to one in a way that lets a high scholarship band read as corroboration of an effect.
forbiddenJoins: scholarshipBand × any efficacy, potency, power or 'works' column
scholarshipBand × any 'recommended', 'canonical practice' or 'start here for practice' surface
using scholarshipBand as a tiebreak that promotes one rite over another in any operative sense
hardLine.permittedUse: Sorting and filtering a STUDY interface: which texts a reader can actually go and check; where the philology is thick and where it is thin; where the site's own citations rest on a critical edition and where they rest on a Victorian translation the field has superseded (FRAMING §4.4, the stated philological cost).

primaryQuantitativeProbe.why: Chosen over Google Scholar because it is (a) reproducible — anyone can re-run the exact URL and get a number, (b) stable enough to cite, and (c) free of Scholar's citation-stuffing and its inclusion of syllabi, blog mirrors and duplicate PDFs. A count nobody can reproduce is not a method, it is an assertion.
primaryQuantitativeProbe.phraseSemantics: The quoted phrase in title_and_abstract.search is treated as a phrase, not a bag of words. Control: the unquoted `search=Greek magical papyri` returns 688; the quoted title_and_abstract phrase returns 153. The quoted form is the one used throughout.
primaryQuantitativeProbe.whatItCounts: DOI-registered scholarly works (journal articles, book chapters, some monographs, some editions) whose TITLE OR ABSTRACT contains the phrase.
whatItDoesNotCount: works whose relevance is in the body but not the title/abstract — which for humanities philology is most of them
monographs without DOIs, which is a large share of the Indological, Sinological and Judaic book literature
most pre-1970 scholarship, i.e. exactly the era in which the German and French philology on several of these corpora was done
conference volumes and Festschriften from small learned presses (SISMEL, Egbert Forsten, IFP/EFEO, Almqvist & Wiksell, Kaivalyadhama)
articles in non-DOI regional journals (Indian Ayurvedic and yoga journals partially; Japanese Buddhological journals partially; Chinese Daoist-studies journals partially)

documentedBiases.bias: DIACRITIC SENSITIVITY — the single largest silent error in this method
documentedBiases.evidence: title_and_abstract.search "Saradatilaka" = 0. Same probe with "Śāradātilaka" = 8, first hit a review of Bühnemann's Gonda Indological Studies volumes. "Hathapradipika" = 8; "Haṭhapradīpikā" = 18. "Nisvasa" = 1; "Niśvāsa" = 3. "Kularnava" = 9; "Kulārṇava" = 5 (the two sets overlap only partly — neither is a superset).
documentedBiases.consequence: An ASCII-only census of Sanskrit corpora undercounts by roughly 2×, and can return a hard ZERO for a text that has a published edition. Every Indic row here was probed in both forms and both numbers are recorded. Anyone re-running this must do the same.
documentedBiases.unresolved: The site cannot determine the true dedup'd union without pulling full result sets; the two figures are reported side by side rather than summed.

documentedBiases.bias: HOMONYM CONTAMINATION — the count can be almost entirely noise
documentedBiases.evidence: "Heptameron" = 283, of which the first result is 'A Reassessment of Boccaccio's Role in Marguerite de Navarre's Heptameron' (Diffley 1995). The count is measuring French Renaissance literature, not the pseudo-Peter-of-Abano grimoire. "Abulafia" = 672; "Abraham Abulafia" = 128 — the residue is the medievalist David Abulafia and others sharing the surname.
documentedBiases.consequence: Raw counts for Heptameron and Abulafia are recorded as VOID and DISAMBIGUATED respectively. Any row whose count was not sampled for contamination is marked sampled:false and must not be ranked on.

documentedBiases.evidence: "Key of Solomon" = 48; a sample of the first five returns 'The Key of Solomon the King' (1989), 'The Key of Solomon the King (Clavicula Salomonis)' (2012), 'Key of Solomon' (2017), 'Key of Solomon' (2012), 'English Translation of The Key of Solomon' (2026) — five reprints of the text, zero pieces of scholarship.
documentedBiases.consequence: For popular grimoires the count measures REPRINT VOLUME, which correlates with occult-market demand and not with scholarly investment. This inverts the axis if used naively: the Key of Solomon outscores the Niśvāsa 48 to 3, and the truth is the exact opposite.

documentedBiases.evidence: "hatha yoga" = 1722 and "rasashastra" = 512. These are dominated by contemporary clinical-trial and pharmacology literature (yoga-intervention RCTs; modern Ayurvedic bhasma pharmacognosy), not by philology. A sample of "Gheranda" = 79 returns modern comparative-practice papers ('A COMPARATIVE STUDY OF SHATKARMA ACORDING TO GHERANDA SAMHITA AND HATHA YOGA PRADIPIKA', 2023) alongside Mallinson's edition.
documentedBiases.consequence: For the haṭha and rasaśāstra rows the corpus-level count is recorded but explicitly disqualified as a philology proxy. The narrow text-level probes (Haṭhapradīpikā, Khecarīvidyā, Śiva Saṁhitā) are used instead.

documentedBiases.bias: ENGLISH-ONLY SEARCHING SYSTEMATICALLY UNDERCOUNTS — measured, not asserted
evidence: German: "Zauberpapyri" = 52 against English "Greek magical papyri" = 153 and Latin-titled "Papyri Graecae Magicae" = 74. Roughly a third again of the literature sits behind a German keyword.

Japanese: "密教" (mikkyō) = 1602 against "Shingon" = 731. The Japanese-language esoteric-Buddhist literature is over twice the English-keyword count, and this is still a floor because much of it is in non-DOI Japanese journals.

French/Italian: not separately probed. Véronèse's Ars notoria edition (SISMEL, Micrologus Library) and Coulon's al-Būnī work are both French-language and both invisible to an English keyword; the Ritter–Plessner Picatrix is German.
documentedBiases.consequence: FOR SEVERAL OF THESE CORPORA THE PRIMARY SCHOLARSHIP IS NOT IN ENGLISH. Shingon ritual manuals, Daoist neidan, the Solomonic Latin tradition, al-Būnī and the Greek magical papyri all have their centre of gravity in Japanese, Chinese, French, Italian or German. Any ranking built on English counts alone will systematically demote them, and the demotion is an artefact of the instrument.

documentedBiases.bias: ABSTRACT COVERAGE IS PATCHY IN THE HUMANITIES
documentedBiases.evidence: OpenAlex inherits abstracts from Crossref; humanities publishers deposit them inconsistently. Where the abstract is missing, only the title is searchable, which shrinks recall further and unpredictably.
documentedBiases.consequence: All counts are FLOORS, not estimates. The correct reading of '4' for Khecarīvidyā is 'at least 4, probably a low multiple of 4' — not 'exactly 4'.

documentedBiases.evidence: api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic="Papyri Graecae Magicae"&rows=0 returns total-results = 6368 — Crossref's bibliographic query is a fuzzy OR-match and does not honour phrases. It is recorded here so the next round does not waste the attempt.
documentedBiases.consequence: Crossref counts are NOT used anywhere in this file.

qualitativeSignals.note: The counts are the weak signal. These three are the strong ones, and where they conflict with the counts the counts lose.

signals.why: The strongest single indicator of scholarly investment. A critical edition means someone collated the manuscripts, built a stemma, and staked a career on the text. It is expensive, slow, and almost never done for a text nobody serious cares about.
gradations: critical-edition-modern — collated from manuscripts, apparatus, academic press, post-1950
critical-edition-legacy — pre-1950 collation, still standard, sometimes superseded in part
semi-critical — some manuscript collation, thin or absent apparatus, or a non-academic press with real scholarly apparatus
uncritical-standard — the circulating text is a printed vulgate, lithograph or Victorian translation with no collation
none — no edition of any kind beyond reproductions

signals.why: A named, funded, multi-year programme (ERC / AHRC / DFG / ANR / a university chair / a standing institute) is the difference between a field and a hobby. It also predicts the next decade of output.

Where three to six names recur across the editions, the monographs and the review literature, the field has an identifiable centre. Where no name recurs, the 'literature' is a scatter of one-off treatments and the corpus is effectively unowned.

weightBandScale.type: ordinal, NOT interval — band 4 is not twice band 2
weightBandScale.derivedFrom: criticalEdition (dominant) + researchProgramme + namedScholars; counts used only to break ties and only where sampled for contamination

bands.5: A century or more of philology. Multiple critical editions across languages, a funded programme or standing chair, a self-identified subfield with its own conferences and review literature.
bands.4: A modern critical edition from an academic press, plus an identifiable school of named scholars. No standing programme, or the programme has closed.
bands.3: Either one critical/semi-critical edition OR a substantial monograph literature, but not both; scholarship is real but sparse and often the work of one or two people.
bands.2: No critical edition. The circulating text is a vulgate, lithograph or Victorian translation. A handful of scholarly treatments, usually within surveys of a wider field rather than dedicated to the text.
bands.1: Essentially none. Editing has been done by practitioners or trade presses; academic engagement is incidental and usually reception-history rather than textual study.

weightBandScale.honestNote: The spread on this list runs the full range, and that is the finding. The Greek magical papyri and the Hekhalot literature have entire subfields; the Kulārṇava and the long recension of the Shams al-Maʿārif — both enormously influential, both constantly cited by practitioners — have essentially nothing.

citationVerificationPolicy.rule: Every exemplar citation carries a `verified` field. `web-2026-07-30` means the bibliographic facts were confirmed against a source retrieved in this pass and the retrieval is named. `unverified-this-pass` means the compiler is asserting it from general knowledge and it MUST be checked before it reaches a shipped page.
citationVerificationPolicy.why: FRAMING §1.2 — no claim rests on a work the compiler has not seen. This file cannot fully honour that for every citation in one research pass, so it marks the gap instead of hiding it.
citationVerificationPolicy.noFabricatedIdentifiers: No DOI has been invented. Where a DOI is given it was read out of a retrieved URL. Where none was retrieved, an ISBN, series number or repository handle is given instead, or the identifier field is null.

criticalEdition.note: THERE IS NO CRITICAL EDITION of the Key of Solomon. The circulating English text is S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Key of Solomon the King (1889), a conflation of a handful of British Museum manuscripts by a Golden Dawn founder — exactly the class of witness FRAMING §4.4 says the PD constraint selects for and that modern editions exist to correct, except that here they do not yet exist. Manuscript-tradition work is active but scattered: a Hebrew original is now generally excluded and a Greek archetype posited; the oldest known fragment (2 leaves, Biblioteca capitolare di Trento, c. 1380–1410) was identified by Matteo Cova.

rows.countVerdict: Both probes are poor instruments — this literature is indexed under text names (Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra, Guhyasamāja, Vajrayoginī), under Tibetan titles, and under 'tantra' generally. The counts here are the least trustworthy in the file and should not be ranked on.

programmes.name: 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha
programmes.scale: 25-year mission for the 108-volume Kangyur, 100-year mission for the 224-volume Tengyur; over 165 grants totalling more than US$8.5m to 60+ translation groups; ~25% of the Kangyur freely available in English; first complete English-language catalogue of the Tengyur
programmes.caveat: A translation initiative funded largely by Buddhist philanthropy (Khyentse Foundation), not a philological editing programme. It is a huge investment in ACCESS and a much smaller one in TEXT CRITICISM, and the census must not conflate the two.

rows.honestSpread: Middle, and highly uneven: a handful of tantras have world-class editions while the sādhana literature proper — thousands of texts — is unedited. FRAMING §7.2 also bites hardest here: much of this material is initiation-gated by its own tradition, and that restriction is a dated, sourced fact about the texts, not something the site adjudicates.

aggregateFindings.finding: The spread is real and it is enormous.
aggregateFindings.detail: Band 5 (PGM, Picatrix, Hekhalot, Niśvāsa, Haṭhapradīpikā) sits beside band 1 (Heptameron) and band 2 (Lemegeton, Key of Solomon, Kulārṇava, Shams al-maʿārif). Two of the most famous operative texts in the Western tradition — the Key of Solomon and the Lemegeton — have no critical edition of any kind, while obscure siblings in the same corpus (Ars notoria, Liber iuratus) have excellent ones.

aggregateFindings.finding: Fame and philology are close to uncorrelated, and where they correlate the sign is sometimes negative.
aggregateFindings.detail: The texts with the largest occult-market presence (Key of Solomon, Lemegeton, Shams al-maʿārif al-kubrā, Kulārṇava) are among the least edited. The count-based probe actively inverts the axis for these, because reprints register as 'works'.

aggregateFindings.finding: For at least six of these corpora the primary scholarship is not in English.
aggregateFindings.detail: Picatrix (German: Ritter–Plessner), Sefer ha-Razim (German: Rebiger–Schäfer), Hekhalot (German: Schäfer), Ars notoria (French: Véronèse), al-Būnī (French: Coulon), Baopuzi (Chinese: Wang Ming), Vijñānabhairava (French: Silburn; Russian: Ivanov), Shingon manuals (Japanese). Measured undercounting for the languages probed: German ≈ +34% of the English figure for PGM; Japanese ≈ 2.2× for esoteric Buddhism; Chinese ≈ 2.0× for neidan.

aggregateFindings.finding: A count-driven ranking would be actively wrong, not merely noisy.
aggregateFindings.detail: Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā: OpenAlex ≈ 1–3, weight band 5. Khecarīvidyā: 4, band 4. Key of Solomon: 48, band 2. Heptameron: 283, band 1. Ranking by count places the two worst-edited texts above the two best-edited. This is why criticalEdition dominates the band and the counts are a tiebreak only.

aggregateFindings.finding: 'Peer reviewed' as an axis label needs qualifying on the page.
aggregateFindings.detail: What is being measured is attention from one academy — largely Euro-American, largely post-1900, largely secular-philological. The Chinese commentarial tradition on the Cantong qi, the Japanese sectarian scholarship on Shingon ritual, and the Sanskrit commentarial tradition on the tantras are all rigorous, cumulative, peer-scrutinised bodies of work that this axis registers at close to zero.

aggregateFindings.finding: This census contains no efficacy information and cannot be made to yield any.
aggregateFindings.detail: Restated because it is the round's hard line: a high band means careful readers, not working magic. There is no field in this file that a downstream renderer could mistake for one, and joining it to one is listed under hardLine.forbiddenJoins.

reproducibility.howToRerun: For each row's `counts[].query`, issue GET https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=title_and_abstract.search:"<query>"&per-page=1 and read meta.count. Percent-encode the phrase INCLUDING its diacritics. Re-run both the ASCII and diacritic forms for every Indic row. Sample the first five results (add &per-page=5&select=title,publication_year) before trusting any count above ~40.
reproducibility.expectedDrift: OpenAlex grows continuously; these figures will rise. They are floors as of 2026-07-30 and should be re-run, not carried forward, if this axis is ever displayed with numbers.
reproducibility.displayRecommendation: Display the BAND and the critical-edition status. Do NOT display the raw counts as a headline number without the contamination note attached in the same DOM node — the Heptameron and Key of Solomon rows show what happens when a count travels without its caveat (cf. FRAMING §5 A-5, the harm note travelling inside the same container).
